MEXICO CITY, Mexico (CNN) -- The driver of a truck that collided with a bus in northeast Mexico, killing 12 people including 11 passengers from the United States and Canada, was intoxicated, a Mexican official said Tuesday. Emergency workers wheel a crash victim on a gurney after Monday's bus crash in Mexico. The tractor-trailer's 21-year-old driver was among those hospitalized after Monday's crash near Monterrey, Mexico, said Segismundo Doguin Martinez, a police official in the Mexican state of Coahuila. The driver of the bus was among those killed, and 15 bus passengers were injured. The Senda Express bus, operated by Grupo Senda, had been traveling from McAllen, Texas, carrying tourists to Zacatecas in central Mexico. Eight of those who died were from the United States, three were from Canada and one, the bus driver, was from Mexico, Doguin said.  Watch rescuers work at scene of deadly crash » . The survivors, most of them in grave condition, were taken to the Christus Muguerza Hospital and the Clinica La Concepcion, the Mexican official said. "They are in a delicate state but out of danger," Doguin said. El Milenio newspaper reported on its Web site that eight of the injured are from the United States, four are from Canada and three from Mexico. Seven of the injured Americans are from Texas and one is from Iowa, the newspaper said. El Norte newspaper's Web site and El Porvenir said the dead and injured included tourists. Among those killed in the crash was 73-year-old Ronald Christy, said his daughter, Pam Fordyce. Christy's wife, Margaret Christy, was in critical condition in a Mexican hospital, Fordyce said. "He was doing exactly what he loved -- traveling," Fordyce, of Altoona, Iowa, told CNN by telephone Tuesday. "He was right where he would want to be, on a bus." She said the couple wintered in Texas and lived in West Liberty, Iowa, in the summer. The U.S. consulate called her at 1:30 a.m. Tuesday to tell her that her father had been killed, Fordyce said, and then followed up with an e-mail with photographs of the crash. "I didn't even know he was on a bus," she said. "I guess I could believe [the consulate] when I talked to my brother" who knew the couple was traveling, she said. "Until then you don't want to believe anything." Doguin, the Mexican official, said the accident occurred when a truck driver went off the road and then overcorrected and swerved into oncoming traffic, hitting the bus. Video of the scene from CNN affiliate TV Azteca 13 showed the left side of the bus sheared off and the semi's cab completely flattened. Rescue efforts took five hours, TV Azteca 13 reported. The U.S. consulate in Monterrey will not release the names of the dead or injured until all family members have been notified, said consulate spokesman Todd Huizinga. "On Monday evening, staff from the consulate in Monterrey went to the Christus Muguerza Hospital to offer assistance to some of the injured who were brought there after the crash," Huizinga said. "The consulate expects to have more detail in the coming hours." The truck driver was injured and is being held by authorities at a hospital, Doguin said. The Web site for Grupo Senda says the company started in Linares, Mexico, more than 75 years ago. It provides bus service to 15 Mexican states and the Texas Valley, the site says. Elizabeth Suarez, director of the McAllen Central Bus Station, where the bus trip originated, issued a statement saying, "We are very saddened by the news this morning. We offer our condolences to the families. The city of McAllen is the landlord of the bus terminal facility in McAllen. Grupo Senda is our tenant." CNN's Melanie Whitley, Taylor Gandossy, Tess Eastment and Monica Trevino contributed to this report from Atlanta, Georgia.

outputs.L1:
MEXICO CITY, Mexico (CNN) — The driver of a truck that collided with a bus in northeastern Mexico, killing 12 people — including 11 passengers from the United States and Canada — was intoxicated, a Mexican official said Tuesday.

Emergency workers wheeled a crash victim on a gurney after Monday’s bus crash in Mexico. The tractor-trailer’s 21-year-old driver was among those hospitalized following the crash near Monterrey, said Segismundo Doguin Martinez, a police official in the Mexican state of Coahuila.

The bus driver was among those killed, and 15 bus passengers were injured. The Senda Express bus, operated by Grupo Senda, had been traveling from McAllen, Texas, carrying tourists to Zacatecas in central Mexico.

Eight of those who died were from the United States, three were from Canada, and one — the bus driver — was from Mexico, Doguin said.

Survivors, most of them in grave condition, were taken to Christus Muguerza Hospital and Clinica La Concepcion, the Mexican official said.

“They are in a delicate state but out of danger,” Doguin said.

El Milenio newspaper reported on its website that eight of the injured were from the United States, four were from Canada, and three were from Mexico. Seven of the injured Americans were from Texas and one was from Iowa, the newspaper said.

El Norte newspaper’s website and El Porvenir reported that the dead and injured included tourists.

Among those killed in the crash was 73-year-old Ronald Christy, according to his daughter, Pam Fordyce. Christy’s wife, Margaret Christy, was in critical condition in a Mexican hospital, Fordyce said.

“He was doing exactly what he loved — traveling,” Fordyce, of Altoona, Iowa, told CNN by telephone Tuesday. “He was right where he would want to be, on a bus.”

She said the couple spent winters in Texas and lived in West Liberty, Iowa, during the summer.

The U.S. consulate called her at 1:30 a.m. Tuesday to inform her that her father had been killed, Fordyce said, and later followed up with an email containing photographs of the crash.

“I didn’t even know he was on a bus,” she said. “I guess I could believe [the consulate] when I talked to my brother,” who knew the couple was traveling, she said. “Until then, you don’t want to believe anything.”

Doguin said the accident occurred when the truck driver went off the road, then overcorrected and swerved into oncoming traffic, striking the bus.

Video from the scene, provided by CNN affiliate TV Azteca 13, showed the left side of the bus sheared off and the semi’s cab completely flattened. Rescue efforts took five hours, TV Azteca 13 reported.

The U.S. consulate in Monterrey will not release the names of the dead or injured until all family members have been notified, said consulate spokesman Todd Huizinga.

“On Monday evening, staff from the consulate in Monterrey went to the Christus Muguerza Hospital to offer assistance to some of the injured who were brought there after the crash,” Huizinga said. “The consulate expects to have more detail in the coming hours.”

The truck driver was injured and is being held by authorities at a hospital, Doguin said.

Grupo Senda’s website says the company was founded in Linares, Mexico, more than 75 years ago. It provides bus service to 15 Mexican states and the Texas Valley, according to the site.

Elizabeth Suarez, director of the McAllen Central Bus Station, where the bus trip originated, issued a statement saying, “We are very saddened by the news this morning. We offer our condolences to the families. The city of McAllen is the landlord of the bus terminal facility in McAllen. Grupo Senda is our tenant.”

CNN’s Melanie Whitley, Taylor Gandossy, Tess Eastment, and Monica Trevino contributed to this report from Atlanta, Georgia.

The newspaper El Milenio reported on its website that eight of the injured were Americans, four were Canadians and three were Mexicans. According to the newspaper, seven of the injured U.S. citizens were from Texas and one was from Iowa. ## Fatal Senda Express crash in Mexico leaves families searching for answers

**McALLEN, Texas / NUEVO LEÓN, Mexico —** A cross-border bus trip operated by Senda Express ended in tragedy in northern Mexico when the coach crashed on a highway route used by travelers moving between Texas and the Mexican interior, killing multiple passengers and sending others to hospitals with serious injuries, according to Mexican news reports and broadcast footage from the scene.

The crash drew attention on both sides of the border because the bus line serves passengers traveling through the Rio Grande Valley, including from McAllen, Texas, to destinations in Mexico. In the hours after the wreck, relatives sought information at terminals, hospitals and government offices as authorities worked to identify victims and determine what caused the accident.

Mexican newspapers reported that the Senda Express bus was carrying passengers through northern Mexico when it was involved in a fatal highway crash. Early accounts described a chaotic scene, with emergency crews, police and civil protection personnel responding to the wreckage and transporting survivors to area medical facilities. Officials were still working to reconcile passenger lists with hospital admissions and fatalities, a common difficulty in major bus accidents where travelers may carry limited identification or board at different points along a route.

Footage aired by **TV Azteca** showed the aftermath of the crash: damaged bus wreckage, emergency vehicles gathered along the roadway and rescue workers moving through the scene. The images underscored the severity of the collision and the urgency facing first responders as they searched for survivors and recovered victims. The footage also showed the kind of difficult terrain and highway conditions that can complicate rescue operations in rural or semi-rural areas of northern Mexico.

Mexican newspapers covering the crash reported that investigators were examining the circumstances of the collision, including the condition of the highway, the bus’s route, traffic conditions and whether another vehicle was involved. Authorities typically review driver logs, mechanical records, passenger manifests and roadway evidence in the aftermath of a fatal commercial-bus accident. No final determination of cause had been publicly released in the immediate aftermath.

Hospitals that received the injured were placed under pressure as emergency departments treated passengers with trauma injuries, including fractures, burns, head injuries and internal injuries. Family members gathered outside medical centers seeking confirmation that relatives had survived. In such incidents, hospitals often limit public information because of privacy rules and the need to verify identities before notifying next of kin.

A statement attributed to the **Senda Express bus station in McAllen** said staff were aware of the crash and were working to obtain information about passengers and assist relatives seeking updates. The station urged families to contact the company directly for official information rather than rely solely on rumors circulating on social media or by word of mouth. For many families in South Texas and northern Mexico, bus travel is a routine connection across the border, and the crash immediately raised concerns among those with loved ones traveling on Senda routes.

Senda Express, part of a well-known regional bus network serving Mexico and parts of Texas, has long carried passengers between U.S. border cities and Mexican destinations. The company’s cross-border routes are commonly used by Mexican nationals, U.S. residents visiting family, workers, students and older passengers who prefer bus service to long-distance driving. The crash also highlighted the risks of long-distance bus travel in Mexico, where passengers may travel overnight or across extended rural highway corridors. Mexican federal and state authorities have periodically increased inspections after serious accidents, but enforcement can vary by region and route.

For relatives, the official investigation was secondary to a more immediate need: finding loved ones. Others waited at terminals for confirmation from Senda personnel or Mexican authorities.

Consular officials are often involved when crashes affect passengers with ties to the United States, particularly in border states. In fatal accidents, U.S. authorities may assist families with locating relatives, communicating with hospitals or repatriating remains, while Mexican prosecutors retain jurisdiction over the crash investigation.

The final death toll and the identities of those killed were expected to be confirmed by Mexican authorities after family notifications were completed. Survivors’ conditions also remained subject to change as hospitals continued treatment.
